paragraphs: Biology is the study of living things, from a single bacterium to a whole meadow. People study it to understand how bodies work, why illnesses spread, where food comes from and what happens to wild places when something in them changes.

This course starts small and works outwards in four parts. It opens inside a cell, with its parts, the way substances cross its boundary and the chemistry that keeps it running. Next it follows energy and information: how a leaf catches light, how a cell uses fuel, how DNA is copied and how cells divide. The third part asks how features pass from parents to offspring and how a population changes over generations. The last widens to food webs and the limits on how far a population can grow.
Each lesson tells one idea as a short story, with problems that use small numbers, percentages and simple ratios, so you predict what will happen before you check.
outcomes: You'll be able to tell a bacterium from an animal or plant cell and say what each main part does.
You'll be able to predict which way water and dissolved substances move across a membrane.
You'll be able to follow energy and carbon through a leaf and through a cell that uses fuel.
You'll be able to work out the chance that offspring inherit a trait from a simple cross.
You'll be able to read a food web and calculate how much energy reaches each level.
prerequisites: You should be comfortable with basic arithmetic and percentages; no biology is assumed.
